title: 1992 Los Angeles riots
description: Riots and protests following the beating of Rodney King
wiki_lead:
Los Angeles, California, experienced a series of riots and civil disturbances from April 29 to May 3, 1992. Civil unrest began in South Central Los Angeles on April 29, after a jury acquitted four officers of the Los Angeles Police Department (LAPD) charged with using excessive force in the arrest and beating of Rodney King. The incident, which had been videotaped by George Holliday, who was a bystander to the incident, was heavily reported on by various news and media outlets, such as CNN.
The rioting took place in several areas in the Los Angeles metropolitan area and throughout Orange County, California, as thousands of people rioted over six days following the verdict's announcement. Widespread looting, assault, and arson occurred during the riots, which local police forces had difficulty controlling. The situation in the Los Angeles area was resolved after the California National Guard, United States military, and several federal law enforcement agencies deployed more than 10,000 of their armed responders to assist in ending the violence and unrest.
When the riots ended, 55 people had been killed, 11 of them by the police or National Guard, 2,383 had been injured, more than 12,000 had been arrested, and estimates of property damage were over $1 billion, making it the most destructive period of local unrest in US history. Koreatown, situated just to the north of South Central LA, was disproportionately damaged because of racial tensions between the Black and Korean communities. Much of the blame for the extensive nature of the violence was attributed to LAPD chief of police Daryl Gates, who had already announced his resignation by the time of the riots, for failure to de-escalate the situation and overall mismanagement.

Background


Policing in Los Angeles
Before the release of the Rodney King videotape, minority community leaders in Los Angeles had repeatedly complained about harassment and use of excessive force against their residents by Los Angeles Police Department (LAPD) officers. Daryl Gates, Chief of the LAPD from 1978 to 1992, has been blamed for the riots. According to one study, "scandalous racist violence... marked the LAPD under Gates' tempestuous leadership." Under Gates, the LAPD had begun Operation Hammer in April 1987, which was a large-scale militarized push in Los Angeles.
The city, like other large metropolitan areas in the United States, was also largely affected by a wave of crime due to the crack epidemic in the United States, the Crips–Bloods gang war and an intensification of the war on drugs.
The origin of Operation Hammer can be traced to the 1984 Olympic Games held in Los Angeles. Under Gates' direction, the LAPD expanded gang sweeps for the duration of the Olympics. These were implemented across wide areas of the city but especially in South Central and East Los Angeles, areas of predominantly minority residents. grok_lead: The 1992 Los Angeles riots erupted as widespread violence, looting, arson, assault, and homicide in parts of Los Angeles County, California, starting on April 29, 1992. They followed a jury in Simi Valley acquitting four Los Angeles Police Department officers of state charges for severely beating African American motorist Rodney King during a March 1991 traffic stop and chase. Unrest began in South Central Los Angeles, a neighborhood with poverty rates over 30%, high violent crime, deindustrialization, and gang activity. It escalated over five to six days, spreading to Koreatown, Hollywood, and areas with large black and Latino populations. The riots resulted in 63 deathsâ10 from police gunfire, most from civilian homicides, assaults, and arson âplus 2,383 hospitalizations, over 12,000 arrests, and about 3,600 fires destroying more than 1,000 structures for roughly $1 billion in damage. RAND Corporation analysis of peak-day arrests showed diverse participants skewed to the local underclass: 51% Latino, 36% African American. This highlighted multi-ethnic violence, not just racial uprising. Targets included Korean American merchants, who armed themselves on rooftops as "Rooftop Koreans," amid tensions like the 1991 shooting of black teenager Latasha Harlins by a Korean store owner. Governor Pete Wilson declared a state of emergency on April 29, deploying over 10,000 National Guard troops by May 1. President George H.W. Bush federalized 4,000 reservists and sent U.S. Marines. Order returned by May 4. The events revealed issues like eroded community norms, welfare dependency, and policing strains in high-crime areas, where South Central's pre-riot homicide rate exceeded 50 per 100,000 annually. Economic models of riot participationâfactoring enforcement gaps and low detection risksâframe the unrest as opportunistic social breakdown amid local grievances and urban decay, not coordinated protest.
